title: MemEvolve: Meta-Evolution of Agent Memory Systems
one_liner: The paper evolves not only what an agent remembers but also how its memory system is built, so different tasks can end up with different memory rules, storage layouts, and retrieval behavior.
lead: Many agent systems now improve over time by storing experience, but most of them keep the same memory design forever. That means the agent can add new facts and tools while still being stuck with a fixed way of encoding, storing, fetching, and pruning them. This paper treats the memory system itself as something that can evolve, because a task that needs compact procedural notes may want a very different memory design from a task that needs long evidence trails or reusable code fragments.

problem.h2: A fixed memory design cannot fit every agent task
paras: An agent memory system has at least four jobs: write experience into memory, decide what form to store, fetch the right past item later, and clean up old material. Different tasks stress those jobs differently. Web search may need concise reusable snippets, while long tool workflows may need detailed traces with failure notes.

When one hand-designed memory architecture is used for every setting, the agent learns inside a narrow box. It can gather more experience, but it cannot change the memory rules that decide what gets kept and what gets resurfaced. That slows adaptation because a poor memory design keeps feeding the planner the wrong kind of support.

callout.html: The memory contents can improve while the memory machinery stays wrong, so the paper evolves both together because a bad write or fetch rule can keep hiding the useful experience the agent already collected.

panels.title: 1. Fixed memory system
panels.viz_args: One write rule, one fetch rule, one cleanup rule
panels.caption: The usual setup gives every task the same memory machinery.

panels.title: 2. Task changes
panels.viz_args: Search task wants short notes. Coding task wants detailed traces.
panels.caption: Different tasks need different memory behavior.

panels.title: 3. Evolve memory modules
panels.caption: Encoding, storage, retrieval, and cleanup choices mutate and recombine.

panels.title: 4. Keep designs that solve tasks with fewer trials
panels.viz_args: Good memory design survives because it supports better decisions
panels.caption: Selection is based on agent success and interaction cost.

panels.title: 5. Task-matched memory system
panels.caption: The final agent uses a memory setup shaped by the task instead of a generic template.

steps.text: Break memory design into parts such as write rule, storage form, fetch rule, and cleanup rule.
Create different combinations of those parts so the agent can try multiple memory designs.
Evaluate each memory design by how well the agent solves tasks and how many interactions it spends.

steps.b: Select and mutate the better designs
steps.text: Keep memory systems that help the agent solve more with less effort, because those designs are task-matched.
Carry the stronger memory system into new runs and related tasks, because the search is trying to keep designs that surface useful support reliably.

paras: The paper changes the optimization target from 'learn better contents inside a fixed memory box' to 'learn better contents and a better memory box at the same time.' The explicit object of search is the modular memory architecture itself, because the architecture decides which experiences are kept, how they are organized, and when they are returned to the planner.

hidden.name: memory-task fit
paras: Memory-task fit measures how well a particular memory design matches the structure of the task. A good fit means the memory writes the right level of detail, fetches the right past cases at the right time, and forgets material that would only distract the planner.

This is the quantity the paper is really chasing, because task performance rises when the memory system surfaces the right support with low interaction cost. The memory system itself is therefore treated as a variable to optimize, not as a fixed background choice.

cells: design locks onto one benchmark only
heat.caption: Darker means the memory design is better matched to the task's real support needs.

reads.html: A good memory system stores the right things in the right form and brings them back at the right time for the current task.
MemEvolve searches over modular memory architecture choices so that encoding, storage, retrieval, and management policies adapt with task demands.

mechanism.h2: Why evolving the memory system helps
paras: A fixed memory design bakes in assumptions about what evidence matters. If those assumptions are wrong for a task, the agent keeps retrieving the wrong support no matter how many episodes it survives. Evolving the memory architecture helps because it lets the system change the write and fetch rules that created the mismatch in the first place.

The modular setup makes search feasible. Instead of redesigning memory from scratch, the method swaps and recombines interpretable parts such as how summaries are written, how experiences are grouped, and how old material is dropped. That works because each part contributes a specific behavioral change that can be tested quickly.

Selection on both success and interaction count matters because a memory design that solves tasks only after many extra trials is not truly good support. The better memory systems are the ones that help the agent reach solutions sooner by resurfacing useful past experience at the point of need.

stages.s: Task family plus modular memory design space
Assemble candidate write, store, fetch, and cleanup rules
Run agents with each memory design on real tasks
Score task success and interaction cost
Keep, mutate, and recombine strong memory designs
Task-matched memory architecture for future runs

math.h2: The equation for selecting memory designs
math.words: A memory design is favored when it solves more tasks and uses fewer interactions, because the search wants support systems that are both effective and economical.
symbols: how often the agent completes its tasks with a given memory design
how strongly the search penalizes extra environment interactions
the amount of trial-and-error the agent spends while using that memory design
score used to keep or discard a memory architecture

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Design A solves 8 of 10 tasks and needs 30 interaction units.
Design B solves 7 of 10 tasks and needs 10 interaction units.
If cost weight is 0.1, design A gets 8 - 0.1 * 30 = 5.
Even though A solves one more task, B is selected because it reaches strong performance with much lower interaction cost.
Over many rounds, this pushes the search toward memory systems that provide the right support sooner.

math.note: The score captures the paper's main tradeoff: memory is good only when it improves task solving enough to justify the interaction budget it consumes, because extra memory work is worthwhile only if it reduces enough failed trials.

charts.title: Fixed memory template
charts.note: A one-size memory system helps some tasks but keeps mismatch costs on others, because the same write and fetch rules cannot serve every task equally well.

charts.title: Meta-evolved memory system
charts.note: The gains come from changing the memory machinery itself so the planner sees more relevant support with less wasted retrieval.

items.html: If there are too many memory module combinations, the evolution loop may spend large effort exploring weak designs before it reaches a good one.
A memory design can look strong on one task family yet fail elsewhere if the search rewards narrow tricks instead of general support behavior.
If task scores are noisy, the search may keep or discard designs for the wrong reason, because fitness reflects randomness instead of genuine memory quality.
The method is strongest when candidate modules are interpretable, evaluation spans several related tasks, and fitness balances success against interaction cost.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build two simple agent tasks: one that benefits from short reusable notes and one that benefits from longer execution traces. Define a small modular memory space with alternative write, fetch, and cleanup rules, then evolve those designs across repeated runs.

Compare the evolved memory systems with a fixed baseline. The evolved systems should solve more tasks with fewer retries because each task ends up with a memory design whose storage and retrieval behavior matches what the planner actually needs.
demo.metric_eq: fitness = solved_tasks - cost_weight * retry_count and transfer_score = solved_related_tasks / total_related_tasks
demo.closing: The demo should show that changing memory contents alone is not enough when the underlying memory rules are poorly matched to the task.
